Recursion
Base and recursive cases in JavaScript, stack overflow in deep recursion, why not to rely on tail calls, and how a trampoline keeps the stack from growing.
Learn to write recursive functions with a base case and a recursive case, and understand why deep recursion in JS overflows the stack and how a trampoline avoids it.
text
Recursion is the ability of a function to call itself.
Recursion must meet two basic requirements in order to work correctly.
list
The base case. This is the logic at which the recursion must stop — the base condition that stops the function from calling itself.
The recursive case. This is the logic in which the function calls itself, usually with small changes to the arguments.
Recursion is frequently used in functional programming.

The "rateSum" function in the example above has one significant drawback: each call waits for the result of the next one so it can add its own number to it. So the depth of the call stack grows with the length of the array. Let's see what tail recursion changes here.

Why do we need this? Until a call finishes, its frame (arguments, local variables and the place to return the result to) stays on the call stack. The stack size is limited, so on a large array synchronous recursion fails with a stack overflow error (in Chrome and Node.js it is RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded).

A tail call does not reduce the number of calls. It lets the engine drop the caller's stack frame: ES2015 requires this in strict mode (proper tail calls), and then the stack depth does not grow. Among browser engines, only JavaScriptCore (Safari) implements it; V8 (Chrome, Node.js) had it behind a flag and removed it, and SpiderMonkey (Firefox) does not have it. That is why deep recursion in JS needs a trampoline. In production code, don't rely on tail recursion unless you know exactly how many calls there will be.
Further on in the recursion section we will use techniques that let you safely use recursion in production code without counting the number of calls.
So how do we free up the call stack without overflowing it in production code?
Make the code asynchronous, avoid blocking the thread, and free up the stack

Use a trampoline. A thunk is a function with no arguments that defers a computation; a trampoline is a loop that keeps calling thunks while the result is a function. The recursive calls turn into a loop, so the stack does not grow.
Let's examine the logic of using a trampoline to avoid stack overflow. The trampoline works synchronously, unlike a call through a timer.
Let's look at the main principles of the trampoline.
A trampoline is a wrapper function that gives our main function special behavior.
The trampoline function returns another function that accepts arguments.
Inside, it calls the main function once with these arguments.
While the returned value is a function, the trampoline calls it in a loop. As soon as the result is not a function, the loop stops and the trampoline returns the result.
In the base case the main function must return a result.
In the recursive case the main function must return a function with no arguments (a thunk) that performs the next step.
Recursion needs two cases: the base case stops the calls, and the recursive case calls the function again, usually with small changes to the arguments.
Until a call finishes, its frame stays on the call stack. The stack size is limited, so on a large array synchronous recursion fails with a stack overflow.

A tail call does not reduce the number of calls. ES2015 requires the engine to drop the caller's stack frame only in strict mode (proper tail calls), and among browser engines only JavaScriptCore (Safari) implements it. So production code should not rely on tail recursion unless you know exactly how many calls there will be.
You can free the stack by running the recursive step asynchronously through a timer: the thread is not blocked, but such code is slow.

A trampoline works synchronously: in the recursive case the function returns a thunk, a function with no arguments holding the next step, and the trampoline calls these functions in a loop while the result is a function. The stack does not grow.
